claim: On 7 October 2022 the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule (87 FR 62186) amending the Export Administration Regulations to control advanced computing integrated circuits and semiconductor manufacturing items destined for China.
evidence: "BIS is amending the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to implement necessary controls on advanced computing integrated circuits (ICs), computer commodities that contain such ICs"; "BIS imposes new export controls on certain semiconductor manufacturing items and activities involving the 'development' or 'production' of advanced integrated circuits" (Federal Register 2022-21658, Summary; citation 87 FR 62186; provisions effective October 7 and October 21, 2022)

claim: The October 2022 BIS rule requires US persons to obtain a licence for certain activities that support the development or production of certain ICs in China.
evidence: "BIS is also informing the public that specific activities of 'U.S. persons' that 'support' the 'development' or 'production' of certain ICs in the PRC require a license." (Federal Register 2022-21658, Summary)

claim: The October 2022 BIS rule created two new Foreign Direct Product rules for advanced computing and supercomputers and expanded licence requirements for 28 China-based Entity List entities.
evidence: "this rule creates two new Foreign Direct Product (FDP) rules related to advanced computing and 'supercomputers'"; "this rule expands the scope of licensing requirements for 28 existing entities on the Entity List that are located in China" (Federal Register 2022-21658, Summary)

claim: A BIS interim final rule effective 2 December 2024 (89 FR 96790) added new Foreign Direct Product rules for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, expanded SME controls and created controls on high-bandwidth memory (ECCN 3A090.c).
evidence: paraphrase with partial quote: Federal Register 2024-28270 summary describes two new FDP rules for SME for 'advanced-node integrated circuits' (destined to Macau and Country Group D:5, and to Entity List Footnote 5 entities) and a new ECCN 3A090.c controlling "HBM having a `memory bandwidth density' greater than 2 GB per second per square millimeter." Effective December 2, 2024.

claim: BIS's September 2025 'affiliates rule' made any entity at least 50% owned by Entity List parties automatically subject to Entity List restrictions.
evidence: "any entity that is at least 50 percent owned directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, by one or more entities on the Entity List" (Federal Register 2025-19846, describing the rule published September 30, 2025)

claim: BIS suspended the affiliates rule for one year, from 10 November 2025 through 9 November 2026; as published, it is to be reinstated automatically on 10 November 2026 unless further action is taken (status as of the rule text; not re-checked after publication).
evidence: paraphrase: Federal Register 2025-19846 states the suspension runs from November 10, 2025 through November 9, 2026 and that the requirements will apply again after that date unless further action is taken.
notes: Status changes often; re-verify after 9 Nov 2026.

claim: Effective 15 January 2026, BIS changed its licence review policy for exports to China and Macau of the Nvidia H200 and equivalent or less-advanced AI chips from a presumption of denial to case-by-case review.
evidence: "changing it from a presumption of denial to a case-by-case review"; covers "the Nvidia H200 and its equivalents, as well as less advanced chips"; "The effective date of this rule is January 15, 2026" (Federal Register 2026-00789, Summary). BIS press release 13 Jan 2026: "BIS will now review export license applications for the Nvidia H200, AMD MI325X, and similar chips on a case-by-case basis provided certain security requirements are met."

claim: Case-by-case approval of H200-class chip exports to China requires conditions including independent third-party testing in the US and evidence that exports will not reduce production capacity available to US customers.
evidence: "exporting these products to China will not reduce global semiconductor production capacity currently available to U.S. customers"; "the Chinese purchaser has adopted export compliance procedures, including customer screening"; "the product has undergone independent, third-party testing in the United States to verify its performance and security" (BIS press release, 13 Jan 2026)

claim: On 13 May 2025 BIS announced it would not enforce, and would formally rescind, the January 2025 AI Diffusion Rule, whose compliance date was 15 May 2025.
evidence: paraphrase: BIS press release of May 13, 2025 states that enforcement officials have been instructed not to enforce the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule, that rescission will be formalised through regulation, and references the May 15, 2025 compliance date.
notes: Could not confirm whether a formal rescission rule has since been published in the Federal Register.

claim: Alongside the AI Diffusion Rule rescission, BIS issued guidance on risks of using certain Huawei Ascend chips and on diversion of US AI chips.
evidence: paraphrase: BIS press release (13 May 2025) lists guidance on 'Risks associated with PRC advanced computing integrated circuits, specifically certain Huawei Ascend chips', consequences of US AI chips being used for Chinese AI model training, and supply-chain protection against diversion.

claim: The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 provides the US Department of Commerce with USD 52.7 billion over five years for semiconductor programmes.
evidence: "The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 provides the Department of Commerce with $52.7 billion over five years" (NIST, CHIPS for America Fact Sheet: Federal Incentives)

evidence: "the CHIPS Program Office responsible for $39 billion in incentives to encourage investment in facilities and equipment in the United States"; "the CHIPS Research and Development (R&D) Office responsible for $11 billion to develop a robust domestic R&D ecosystem" (NIST fact sheet)

claim: NIST's CHIPS 'guardrails' rule (15 CFR Part 231, effective 24 November 2023) bars CHIPS funding recipients for ten years from materially expanding semiconductor manufacturing capacity in a foreign country of concern and restricts joint research or technology licensing with foreign entities of concern.
evidence: Covered entities cannot engage in "material expansion of semiconductor manufacturing capacity in a foreign country of concern" for ten years following the award date (Federal Register 2023-20471, 88 FR 65600, 15 CFR Part 231, effective November 24, 2023); technology clawback on joint research/technology licensing with foreign entities of concern is paraphrased from the same summary.

claim: Under 26 USC 48D the advanced manufacturing investment credit applies to facilities whose primary purpose is manufacturing semiconductors or semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and does not apply to property whose construction begins after 31 December 2026.
evidence: "a facility for which the primary purpose is the manufacturing of semiconductors or semiconductor manufacturing equipment"; "The credit allowed under this section shall not apply to property the construction of which begins after December 31, 2026." (26 USC 48D, uscode.house.gov prelim edition)

claim: The section 48D credit rate is 35% of qualified investment following P.L. 119-21 section 70308, with 25% applying to facilities placed in service before 2026.
evidence: "The advanced manufacturing investment credit is equal to 35% of the qualified investment with respect to any advanced manufacturing facility" ... "unless the facility was placed in service before 2026, in which case the credit rate is 25%" (IRS correction to 2025 Form 3468 instructions, citing P.L. 119-21, section 70308)

claim: On 31 March 2025 an executive order created the United States Investment Accelerator within the Department of Commerce and made it responsible for the CHIPS Program Office.
evidence: "The Investment Accelerator shall be responsible for the CHIPS Program Office within the Department of Commerce, which shall focus on delivering the benefit of the bargain for taxpayers by negotiating much better deals than those of the previous administration." (Executive Order 'Establishing the United States Investment Accelerator', 31 March 2025)

claim: In August 2025 the US government agreed to take a 9.9% equity stake in Intel (433.3 million shares at USD 20.47) funded by USD 5.7 billion of unpaid CHIPS Act grants and USD 3.2 billion of Secure Enclave awards.
evidence: "9.9 percent stake in the company"; "433.3 million primary shares of Intel common stock at a price of $20.47 per share"; "the remaining $5.7 billion in grants previously awarded, but not yet paid, to Intel under the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act and $3.2 billion awarded to the company as part of the Secure Enclave program" (Intel Form 8-K Ex. 99.1, filed Aug 2025)

evidence: Our reading of the Investment Accelerator order and the Intel equity agreement; whether equity terms apply to other awardees was not established.

claim: A Section 232 proclamation signed 14 January 2026 imposed a 25% ad valorem duty, effective 15 January 2026, on certain advanced computing chips and derivative products imported into the US.
evidence: paraphrase with partial quote: The proclamation of January 14, 2026 imposes a 25% ad valorem duty on "certain advanced computing chips and certain derivative products" listed in its Annex, effective January 15, 2026 at 12:01 a.m. EST (White House, 'Adjusting Imports of Semiconductors, Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment, and Their Derivative Products into the United States').

claim: The January 2026 Section 232 chip tariff exempts imports for US data centers, repairs, R&D, startups, non-data-center consumer and civil industrial applications, and US public-sector use.
evidence: paraphrase: The proclamation lists exemptions for imports for U.S. data centers, repairs or replacements, research and development, startups, non-data center consumer applications, non-data center civil industrial applications, U.S. public sector use, and other uses the Secretary determines strengthen domestic supply chains.

claim: The January 2026 proclamation said broader tariffs on semiconductors, with a tariff offset programme, may be considered after trade negotiations, and required a market review by 1 July 2026.
evidence: The proclamation states the administration "may consider imposing significant tariffs" on semiconductors broadly with accompanying tariff offset programmes after ongoing negotiations; the Secretary must provide a status update within 90 days and a market review by July 1, 2026 (paraphrase of the surrounding text).

claim: As of 3 September 2026, a second phase of US Section 232 semiconductor tariffs had been publicly signalled by the Commerce Secretary, but no new proclamation, rates or effective date had been published.
evidence: "build in the United States, pay nothing; build nowhere, pay to enter the market" (Lutnick, reported by Tech Times, 3 Sep 2026); article states "No new proclamation has been signed."
notes: Tier-3 only. Status must be re-checked against whitehouse.gov and the Federal Register.

claim: USTR determined under Section 301 that China's targeting of the semiconductor industry is actionable, and imposed additional tariffs on Chinese semiconductors at 0% from 23 December 2025, rising on 23 June 2027 to a rate to be announced.
evidence: "China's targeting of the semiconductor industry for dominance is unreasonable and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce"; "0 percent, increasing in 18 months on June 23, 2027, to a rate to be announced not fewer than 30 days prior to that date" (Federal Register 2025-23912, Notice of Action)

claim: The Section 301 semiconductor investigation was initiated on 23 December 2024 and its action covers 18 tariff lines including wafers, transistors, diodes, thyristors and integrated circuits, on top of an existing 50% Section 301 tariff on Chinese semiconductors.
evidence: paraphrase: Federal Register 2025-23912 states the investigation was initiated December 23, 2024; the action covers 18 semiconductor-related tariff codes (silicon wafers, transistors, diodes, thyristors, ICs and parts) and supplements the existing 50% Section 301 tariff on Chinese semiconductors.

claim: The US Treasury's Outbound Investment Security Program, effective 2 January 2025, prohibits or requires notification of certain investments by US persons in Chinese (incl. Hong Kong and Macau) entities active in semiconductors and microelectronics, quantum and AI.
evidence: Program covers "semiconductors and microelectronics, quantum information technologies, and artificial intelligence"; countries of concern: "the People's Republic of China, along with the Special Administrative Regions of Hong Kong and Macau"; directs Treasury to "establish a program to prohibit or require notification of certain types of outbound investments by United States persons" (Treasury Outbound Investment Program page; effective January 2, 2025)

claim: SEC-reporting companies that use tin, tantalum, tungsten or gold necessary to their products must file an annual Form SD by 31 May on whether those minerals originated in the DRC or adjoining countries.
evidence: "tantalum, tin, gold, or tungsten"; "the Democratic Republic of the Congo ("DRC") or an adjoining country"; "Form SD, a new specialized disclosure form filed with the SEC"; due "on May 31" (SEC Conflict Minerals Disclosure compliance guide)
notes: Applies across manufacturers; chipmakers use these metals, but semiconductor-specific applicability was not separately evidenced.
